Bonhomie means a warm, easy, cheerful friendliness — the quality of being genuinely good-natured in a way that makes everyone around you feel comfortable and welcome.

Think of someone you know who always seems relaxed and pleasant to be around. Not someone who is putting on a performance of being nice, and not someone who is loud and over-the-top, but someone who has a natural, easy warmth that makes any room feel a little lighter the moment they walk in. They smile easily, they make you feel at ease, they are never stiff or cold, and conversations with them flow without effort. That quality — that genuine, sunny, open good-naturedness — is exactly what bonhomie means.

The word is a noun, so it describes a quality or a state. A person can have bonhomie, they can radiate bonhomie, or a social gathering can be full of bonhomie.
What makes bonhomie special — and different from just "friendliness"?

"Friendly" is a fairly flat word. A shop assistant can be friendly. A customer service email can be written in a friendly tone. But bonhomie is richer than that. It carries three things at once:

Warmth — It is genuinely felt, not performed. It comes from inside a person, not from obligation.

Cheerfulness — There is a lightness and good humor to it. A person with bonhomie tends to be pleasantly upbeat and easy to laugh with.

Ease — It is effortless and relaxed. There is nothing strained, nervous, or try-hard about it.

Together, these three things create something more specific than simple friendliness. Bonhomie is the kind of quality that makes people say things like, "He just has a way about him," or "She makes everyone feel instantly at ease."
How it differs from similar words:

Charisma is about magnetic, compelling personal power that draws people toward you — it can even be a little intimidating. Bonhomie is softer and warmer. A charismatic person commands attention; a bonhomous person makes you feel at home.

Joviality is about being jolly, merry, and full of laughter — it leans heavily on the cheerful side. Bonhomie includes that cheerfulness, but it is also warmer and more genuine. Joviality can sometimes feel like a performance; bonhomie almost never does.

Affability means being easy to approach and talk to — it is the closest cousin of bonhomie. But affability is more passive (you are easy to talk to), while bonhomie is more active and alive (you actively radiate warmth and good cheer).
Where you'll see this word used:

Bonhomie is a slightly elevated, literary word. You won't hear it much in casual everyday conversation, but you will see it often in books, journalism, and formal writing when the writer wants to describe someone's personality with precision. If a writer uses this word, they are specifically reaching for that combination of warmth, good humor, and ease — nothing else quite captures it.

"The host greeted every guest with such genuine bonhomie that even the shyest people in the room quickly felt at ease."

"He was well-liked not for his intelligence or his success, but for his natural bonhomie — an openness that made strangers feel like old friends within minutes."

"The small café had a warm atmosphere of bonhomie, with regulars chatting freely across tables as though they had known each other for years."

Notice that in the last example, bonhomie describes not a person but a social atmosphere — the feeling in a room. This is a common and completely correct use of the word. A place, a gathering, or a moment can be full of bonhomie when the warmth and friendliness of the people in it create a shared, cheerful ease.

Bonhomie is the genuine, warm, cheerful, effortless good-naturedness that some people have — and sometimes some places have — that makes everyone around feel comfortable, welcome, and happy to be there.
